Names and Forms of Address.text: Names in Japan are spoken family name first and written that way on official forms, while this world's records list people given name first. Acquaintances, classmates, colleagues and strangers use family name plus a suffix: -san as the polite default, -kun for younger men and male classmates, -chan for small children, close friends and pets, -sama for customers and people of high status, sensei for teachers, doctors and some veteran pros, and senpai for an upperclassman at school or a senior at work. Moving to someone's given name is a real step in a friendship and usually happens by invitation; dropping the suffix shows closeness, or rudeness from a stranger. On the job pros go by their hero names: the public, the press and colleagues say Endeavor or Mount Lady, and a hero's legal name, though on record, is seldom used. Students address teachers by hero name or as sensei. A childhood nickname used by only one person marks a long shared history. Bows replace handshakes: a nod between friends, a deeper bow for thanks, apologies and superiors. Every canon person keeps exactly the forms of address their own record uses.
